title: We live in Singapore and plan to retire in Malaysia. How should we invest in Mont Kiara?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #247 | COUPLE FROM SG INVESTING IN KL
excerpt: A Singaporean with a Malaysian wife wants older Mont Kiara subsale units to start a rental portfolio. Sean says buy for yield, not the lowest price per square foot, and not a home for 20 years' time.

qa.asker: AC, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: AC is Singaporean and works overseas; his Malaysian wife looks after the household full time and has no income. Their rented-out Singapore flat is cash flow positive, and they hope to retire in Malaysia in about 20 years. They have cash for down payments and are looking at older Mont Kiara subsale units under RM1 million, around 1,200 to 1,400 sq ft.
qa.question: Can they get a loan, which units should they buy, and how do they find a good price?
qa.quote: The goal of investment is not to buy the cheapest project.
qa.answer: Buy for investment only, and judge each unit by its rental yield rather than its price per square foot; a newer unit can earn more than a cheaper, bigger old one. Malaysian banks treat a Singaporean's income much like a local's, and good subsale prices go to buyers who have done their research before the deal appears.

reasons.title: Banks will lend on his income
reasons.body: Malaysian banks recognise Singapore income and even CPF statements, with the same rates and tenures as locals. Because his wife has no income, the loan has to be assessed on his, for example with her name on the SPA and both names on the loan agreement.

reasons.title: Yield beats price per square foot
reasons.body: Sean's newer Mont Kiara unit cost about RM1,000 per sq ft and yields about 6.9%, while a larger older unit down the street at about RM600 per sq ft yields about 4.2%. Older layouts with lower ceilings rent less well.

reasons.title: Don't buy a home for 20 years' time
reasons.body: Their needs in 20 years are unknowable: living here as a Singaporean may mean leaving the country regularly unless MM2H rules allow longer stays, and a large landed home can simply be rented then. Buy now purely as an investment.

reasons.title: Good subsale deals reward preparation
reasons.body: Sean bought his unit below the first-phase price from an owner he knew, but only because he already knew the project's prices inside out and had his finances ready. Without that, a broker and patient research are the only routes.

actions: Ask banks how they will assess the loan when the property is in your wife's name but the income is yours.
Compare each shortlisted unit's annual rent divided by its price, and buy the higher yield, not the lower price per square foot.
Compare old and new projects, and nearby areas such as Dutamas and Sri Hartamas, on price per square foot, size, rent and condition before choosing.
Know the recent transacted prices well enough that you can recognise a good deal the moment it is offered.
Get renovation quotes and rents achieved by similar units before you budget for refurbishing an older unit.
qa.caveat: Mont Kiara strategies don't carry over to Johor Bahru, where buyers earning Singapore dollars favour landed homes near the checkpoints. Sean also notes that older Mont Kiara buildings are generally well maintained, but one heavily used for short stays in the Dutamas area is an exception.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #247. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in April 2024. The episode was sponsored by OpenHouse, an app developed by Sean's friends. Sean works with The Makeover Guys, a renovation company, and is a client (not the owner) of FAR Capital, a property investment club he recommends in this episode; the article leaves out his referral links.
